1:
The dating is fixed differently by each voice that attempts it. Gill reports a Jewish chronicle placing the murder on the third day of the seventh month, fifty-two days after the destruction of the temple, and notes the fast afterwards kept on that account, then gives two rival reckonings, one putting it on the first day, the new year, with the fast held the day after because the first was a festival, and the historian's account dating it thirty days after the warning was given. Clarke names only the month, answering to the first new moon of our October. Wesley and Ellicott both measure from the capture of the city and make it three months. Ellicott adds a reconstruction of the visit's purpose, that it purported to be one of courtesy and recognition, the remaining representatives of the royal house showing themselves ready to welcome the new governor, and since the month included the feast of tabernacles they may have come as if to share its festivities.

Why the crime is so black is answered chiefly by the two who moralise. Calvin puts the weight on hospitality: even the heathen held it sacred and counted its violation the greatest atrocity, with a god of hospitality reserved to avenge an oath broken at table; and this man had sworn fidelity, was received again, was treated as a son by a host who had acted a father's part, and rose from that table to kill him. He then traces the motive to birth. The royal seed was in deepest disgrace, the king's children slain and the king himself blinded and led away bound, yet those once in dignity can hardly relinquish the high notions that inflate them, so that reduced to want they still aim at something royal and will not submit to God; the murderer thought it no honour to himself that another had been set over the people. Henry says something similar in his own register, that the killer was of the seed royal and therefore jealous of a man's greatness and enraged that he should accept a commission from the conqueror, and he stresses the artifice, that they pretended friendship, gave no warning, and watched their opportunity until they had him alone. Clarke supplies the custom that makes the treachery legible: eating bread together was the same as making a solemn covenant, since he who ate with another was ever reputed a friend. Ellicott reaches for a modern parallel instead, a massacre in which guests murdered their host at the very moment he was receiving them with open arms.

How ten men could kill so many is a difficulty two voices take up. Ellicott raises it directly and offers three mitigations: the massacre need not have gone beyond the Jews and officers sharing the hospitality, who like their host may have been surprised unarmed and at meat, and each of the ten princes may have brought his own retinue; he adds two comparable episodes from Greek history and observes that the killing was so complete that nobody escaped to tell of it. Gill declines the historian's larger account, that the killer went out by night and slew all the Jews and soldiers in the city, on the ground that the main body were afterwards carried off captive, and restricts the slaughter to those who resisted or might have avenged the governor. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same restriction from the wording, that only those present in the house are meant and, of the soldiers, only the guard allowed him; they also note a proposed emendation of one verb, judging the change possible but not necessary, and read the clause that follows as the narrator's own reflection on the greatness of the crime, the murder being ascribed to the one man because the ten were simply his executioners. Wesley says only that those about the governor's court were killed.
4:
That nobody yet knew is explained by timing and distance. Gill notes the murder was done in the night, so the second day is the day following, and Wesley limits the ignorance to those living at any distance from the town. The pilgrims are placed by their three home towns, which Gill observes belonged to the northern kingdom, so that even at this remove some religious persons were left there with a great regard for the worship at Jerusalem. Ellicott records that the old Greek gives a different second name, a fortress near the first, which suits the order of the three better than the received text, and notes that the road from all three places ran past the town where they were met. He also notices what they carried: not burnt offerings but the meat offering, cakes of flour with incense.

Why men should be travelling to a ruined temple at all is the question of the tile, and it gets two incompatible answers. Wesley supposes they had not heard the temple was burnt. Calvin names that answer and rejects it: those who give it only seek to escape, and the evasion is not credible, since the burning had happened in the fifth month and these men came not from beyond the sea but from places near at hand, so distance cannot account for ignorance. His own solution is that they knew and came anyway, bringing no victims but only incense and an offering, to testify their piety where they had formerly sacrificed. Ellicott takes a middle course, a pilgrimage of mourning to the ruins, perhaps to keep the feast in hope of finding at least an altar on which their oblations might be presented. On the marks of grief they divide again. Clarke and Wesley take them as the signs of deep mourning used in those countries, probably for the destruction of the city. Ellicott looks for an occasion, either the approaching day of atonement falling in that month or some special fast of the same season, and adds a criticism the others do not make, that the signs themselves are a relapse into a half-heathen custom the law had forbidden.

The meeting on the road is where the treachery is analysed. Gill reconstructs the calculation: hearing that a body of men was on the road in such a habit and on such an errand, he judged it best to go out, stop them and decoy them in, lest they catch some hint of what he had done and raise the country before his design was finished. Clarke reads the weeping as the performance of a felonious hypocrite pretending affliction and wishing to bear them company in their sorrow, and supplies the bait offered, that the governor would appoint them vineyards and fields. Ellicott makes the deception subtler: he does not tell them of the murder but, assuming they have heard of the new appointment, invites them to come and see a man now within whose jurisdiction they stand; and Ellicott adds the textual note that the old Greek makes the pilgrims rather than their host the ones who weep. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the topography, that the road from the north passed close by the town, and give the sequel plainly, that when the men entered the city they were killed and their bodies cast into the pit. Calvin looks instead for the motive and finds none: no war had been declared, no offence given, nothing plotted against him; the likeliest guess is a slight suspicion that they had come to live under the governor's protection, and that one murder would gain him nothing unless he held the whole land. He concludes that wicked men set no bounds to their crimes once begun, and that the sight of such mourners ought to have allayed the fury of any enemy not divested of all sense of equity.
7:
Why the pilgrims were killed at all is answered by nobody with confidence. Ellicott admits the purpose does not appear at first sight and offers four possibilities: their presence as devout mourners may have roused him to bitterness, their willingness to recognise the new governor may have looked like treachery, the deed may have been retaliation for the killing of his kinsmen, or it may have been done for plunder. Calvin, having found no motive at the first murder, again reaches only for a general principle, that once a man has polluted his hands he makes no end of his barbarity. Gill and Clarke concentrate on mechanics instead. Gill adds from the historian that the court was shut as they came in. Clarke reconstructs the plan: the first murder was kept secret, a band of assassins was no doubt lodged in the town, and the eighty were decoyed there so that he would have strength enough to kill them.

The ten who bought their lives are treated as a comment on the killer's character. Wesley puts it briefly, that his covetousness prevailed over his cruelty. Calvin works the thought at length: he was a lion or a wolf or a bear in savageness and at the same time a hungry man, sparing ten of the eighty as soon as he smelt the odour of prey, so that many monsters were in one man; and Calvin guesses that in so disturbed a state he was short of provisions, want making him moderate lest his cruelty cost him something. He adds the harder question the episode raises, why God suffered men who had left their homes to lament the burning of the temple to fall as prey to robbers, and answers only that God has hidden ways of providing for the safety of his people. On the hidden stores themselves the voices are unanimous and practical. Keil and Delitzsch describe them as excavations shaped like cisterns, subterranean granaries whose entrances are so concealed that a stranger's eye could not find them, and note that such places are still universally used in that country. Clarke says the same and gives their local name. Ellicott adds the likely history of the hoard, the produce of the previous year hidden far from habitations while the land was occupied by the invading armies. Whether the ten were kept alive nobody knows: Clarke says it is not recorded, and thinks it likely that once the treasures were in hand they were served as their companions had been.

The pit itself is identified by three voices, with the same king named and different guesses at what he built. Clarke says he made it as a reservoir to supply the place with water, having fortified the town during his war with the northern king. Ellicott gives the fuller history, that the enemy had tried to fortify a rival outpost, that the king of Judah called in Syrian help to compel him to desist and then carried off the stones and timber to strengthen this position; he offers two possibilities for the pit, a trench with a drawbridge built to stop all approach from the neighbouring kingdom, or one of the tanks made to supply a fortress with water; he also records a variant reading turning the phrase about the murdered governor into the pit of that governor, and renders the received phrase literally as by the hand of the governor, his name being used to entrap the unsuspecting. Calvin reconstructs the same war and reasons his way to an inner work: no trench is mentioned in the older account, but it may be inferred, and since this one lay in the middle of the city it was probably a citadel built as a place of refuge, so that if the enemy took the city he could penetrate no further. Gill notes only that the dead were not the eighty.
10:
What the captives were for is guessed at rather than known. Clarke says they were taken to be sold as slaves among the Ammonites. Ellicott reads the seizure as a dynastic gesture: the sons of the king had been killed and the daughters spared and consigned to the governor's care, so that in taking possession of the princesses the murderer asserted, after the fashion of the East, his own claim as representative of the royal house; and since that people had been in alliance with the late king he reckoned on refuge, having in any case been believed sent by their king for the very purpose. Calvin cannot decide whether the plan was formed at the outset or only after the murderer saw he could not hold his ground, though he thinks it settled beforehand, and speculates about the foreign king's interest, that he wished to plant his own people in the emptied land, hoping to rule it and to pacify the conqueror by becoming tributary. He raises two difficulties the others pass over. One is the force required: a few men could not have gathered a people scattered through many towns, so his barbarity must have frightened them and many joined him, an impious faction never wanting followers when hope is offered. The other is the presence of royal daughters at all, when only the poor had been left and the royal seed carried off; he supposes some escaped during the siege, as the murderer himself had.

The pursuit is where the geography is argued. Keil and Delitzsch identify the water as the pool at a town two miles north, one of the large receptacles still found there, and infer that since the place was so near, what had happened must have been known at once and the captains mustered quickly. Ellicott gives the site in more detail, the remains of a large tank on the eastern side of the hill, known from an earlier conflict fought at the same pool, and observes that the halt implies the murderer thought himself safe from attack. He then sets aside the historian's version, placing the encounter at a pool in a town far to the south, on the ground that it would hardly lie on the route to the country he was making for. Calvin works on the name and rejects a conjecture about it: the waters were not called great because rains had lately made them abundant, which he thinks improbable, but because that was the common name. Gill notes that the pursuers took all the soldiers under their command and believed the report at once, having warned the governor and been disregarded.

Henry alone treats the episode as a lesson in timing. He wishes the captains had stayed with the governor after their warning, since they might have been a lifeguard to him and a terror to the murderer and so prevented the bloodshed; instead they were away on some expedition, perhaps not a good one, from which he draws the rule that those who affect to ramble are often out of their place at the moment they are wanted. He calls what follows an after-game. He regrets that the murderers escaped, thinking it strange that vengeance suffered them to live, and notes that the concealment failed as such concealments do. On the flight he observes that a guilty conscience flew in the man's face and he dared not stand against an enemy anything like a match for him, the most cruel being often the most cowardly. On the captives turning about as soon as they saw the rescuers, and finding their own way over while nobody detained them, he draws the plainest moral in the chapter, that those who would be helped must help themselves. Keil and Delitzsch state the same movement without comment, adding only that the captives had followed their captor because they were forced to.
13:
The captives change sides at once and the voices explain why differently. Gill is careful about which people are meant, those brought as prisoners and not the men who had come with the murderer in the first place, and describes the desertion as complete, wheeling off from him without regarding his authority or fearing his menaces, because they were now in sight of the captains and knew them to be friends who had come to deliver them. Clarke gives the reason as weariness of a tyrant and the gladness of finding an opportunity to abandon him. Ellicott finds a different significance in their gladness, that it implies how popular the murdered governor had been and how welcome the prospect of his death being avenged. Calvin locates the cause in the balance of force rather than in feeling: the rescuers came sufficiently armed and were trained soldiers, and their opponent could not be equal to them once the people had gone over.

The escape with eight men is agreed on and counted the same way by two voices. Gill supposes that of the ten who had come, two were killed in the skirmish or taken, or else fled another way. Ellicott draws the same inference more cautiously, that he had come with ten and that two had naturally perished in one or other of the conflicts. Keil and Delitzsch record the escape without comment and pass straight to its consequence.

Why the murderer was allowed to get away is a difficulty Calvin refuses to leave alone, and he is the only voice to raise it. He sets out the case against the escape as strongly as he can: this man had killed not merely a man but the governor, and the very governor by whose protection a remnant had been preserved, and all those found with him, and then seventy more with whom he had no strife, no war and no quarrel; and against such a record stand the plain sentences that he who smites with the sword shall perish by the sword and that whoever sheds man's blood shall have his own blood shed. His answer is that God does not keep one course in his judgments and often prolongs the life of the most wicked, not so that the sentence fails but so that it is executed by other ways; and he takes from a psalm the reason, that the wicked are not to be slain at once lest the people forget, since a punishment executed suddenly is easily forgotten, whereas a man on whom the mark of a curse is impressed and whose life is prolonged is set as though in a theatre to be looked on at leisure. He then argues that the vengeance was in fact carried out. The murder had been committed out of the foolish pride of a royal descent that God had already broken to pieces, and the punishment fitted it: the man arrived before the foreign king a fugitive with eight companions, stripped of the company he had promised, filled with confusion and with no hope of return, and so was despised and cast off, which Calvin thinks was more bitter to him than ten deaths would have been. From this he draws the rule that we are not to form our judgment by the present appearance of things.
16:
Who was in the rescued company is worked out from the list of names for them. Clarke supposes the women, children and eunuchs all belonged to the palace and harem of the last king, some of them his own concubines with their children. Ellicott says the same about the survivors of the harem and adds that the men of war were apparently such as had escaped the first massacre, and guesses at one particular man who may well have been among the eunuchs. Calvin reads the terms as praise before he withdraws it: the word applied to them denotes courage, and the phrase following explains in what the courage lay, that they were warlike men; and he observes that the governor had gathered a considerable number not only from the lower orders but from the higher class. Gill notes only the decision behind the movement, that the captains did not think fit to pursue the fugitive and that the people had committed themselves to their care.

The resting-place is identified through an old benefaction. Clarke names it as the estate given to the son of a Gileadite chief and says the company took it merely as a resting-place, since the design was already to carry everyone into Egypt. Ellicott reconstructs the history behind the name: when the aged chief pleaded his years and declined the king's invitation to court, the offer was transferred to his son, who was afterwards commended to the next king, and it seems probable that part of the royal patrimony as distinct from the royal domains was bestowed on him, and that he perpetuated his gratitude by erecting a resting-place for travellers. Ellicott then suggests an identification the others do not, that this shelter is probably the same as the inn of the Nativity. Keil and Delitzsch work from the philology and the manuscripts: the word occurs only here and must etymologically mean a lodging or caravanserai, and of the two forms of the name in the copies the marginal one is evidently correct, none of the old translators having read the letter that distinguishes the other; they too take the man named to be the son of the Gileadite, supposed to have founded the place for the convenience of travellers.

Why they were afraid is set out plainly and then judged. Keil and Delitzsch tie the clause about the Chaldeans back to the purpose of going into Egypt and give the fear its ground, that after the murderer escaped it was to be feared the conquerors would avenge the governor's death and make those who remained atone for it by execution or deportation. Gill notes that some would join the clause to the previous verse, and takes it as the reason for leaving and settling on the road to Egypt. Ellicott adds the point that makes the fear reasonable rather than merely panicky, that a severe punishment was likely without too careful an inquiry into who had actually been guilty, and that the mere fact of having remained with the murderer might be construed as circumstantial evidence of complicity. Calvin grants the fear was not without reason and then refuses to let it excuse them. They might have sent to the conqueror, thrown the blame on the right person and cleared themselves, and would easily have obtained pardon; the matter could have been settled. Because no fear of God prevailed in them they never considered what was lawful, and were carried into Egypt by a blind impulse, so that their fear was no alleviation of their crime when another remedy lay at hand that God would have blessed. He makes the same judgment of their leader in advance: he was energetic and showed regard for the public good, but he betrayed his unbelief in leading the remnant into Egypt against the prophet's word, so that the chief thing was wanting in him.
